events.title: Chinese memory-maker CXMT claims DRAM production breakthrough
events.summary: ASIA IN BRIEF Chinese memory-maker CXMT, whose products Apple has reportedly evaluated to use in the iPhone, claims to have made a miniaturization breakthrough. The company on Sunday posted news that it has started mass production of chips made with a fifth-generation process that essentially doubles memory density, meaning it can cut twice the number of dies for memory chips from a single wafer. CXMT says its key breakthrough is a high-k dielectric metal gate process – a way of insulating silicon to improve efficiency – adapted to baking DRAM. The company claims its new process puts it on par with rival memory-makers. The proof of the pudding is apparently a pair of LPDDR5X memory modules for smartphones or other high-end consumer electronics. Both products boast 24GB of memory. If CXMT’s claims of improved density and mass production are correct – and the new products aren’t too pricey – it’s good news for Chinese electronics manufacturers who, like their global peers, are struggling to source affordable memory thanks to supply chain crunches caused by demand for AI-related products. That shortage recently saw Apple hike iPhone prices by $100 and led the GSM Association to warn that rising smartphone prices threaten to slow digital inclusion. Democratic governments, however, are mostly uncomfortable with allowing their smartphone manufacturers to use Chinese components. India starts charging fees for instant payments India’s National Payments Corporation (NCP) last week introduced fees to use its Unified Payments Interface (UPI) for the first time. UPI is an instant payment scheme provided by India’s government. It allows transfer of funds between participants, which include over 700 local banks and many e-wallet providers. It also allows person-to-person payments. The scheme is a ubiquitous option even at small retailers across India, and one of the world’s busiest payment schemes with over 24 billion monthly transactions. The scheme is so popular that other payment providers outside India have adopted it so that Indian tourists can use it abroad. UPI launched in 2016 and has until now been free for shoppers and merchants alike. The NCP last week announced it will soon require merchants to pay 0.4 percent fee for when taking payments above 2,000 rupees (£15; $21). India’s government said the charge is needed to fund the operation of the scheme, the cost of which is currently borne by the nation’s government and participating financial institutions. The government ordered merchants not to pass on the fee. China’s online reach is surprisingly short, researcher finds China’s share of content distribution networks is small, leaving Asian nations largely dependent on US companies. That’s the key finding of research by Jason Hung, a quantitative sociologist and research fellow at the Internet Society’s Pulse program. Hung looked up the top 1,000 most popular websites in ten southeast Asian countries (Cambodia, China, Indonesia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Viet Nam) using Google’s Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX), then used three different CDN and IP infrastructure lookup approaches to identify the company and jurisdiction serving the content. “I then used the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) to quantify the severity of market concentration (by service provider and by jurisdiction), where a score above 2,500 is considered highly concentrated, and a maximum score (10,000) means a single actor serves an entire market.” That approach led to the finding that “content delivery in SEA is highly concentrated, with HHI scores ranging from 8,950 to 10,000 across all ten countries.” The researcher found that China-registered companies held no more than 3.9 percent of the CDN market between 2024 and 2026, and that US-registered companies dominated, ranging from 95.9 percent to 99.6 percent. “These findings go beyond what I expected based on my understanding of China’s control over the Global South, especially in Southeast Asia,” he wrote, and leave organizations across the region highly dependent on US tech companies to expose their content to the wider internet. Toyota to hire 400,000 robots Japanese auto-maker Toyota last week told investors it plans to hire 400,000 robots that have two-fingered “hands.” The Embodied Learning robot for Enhanced Yield, aka “ELEY,” is capable of folding a t-shirt and learning how to perform tasks that require considerable manual dexterity. Apparently, the bots needed two weeks to learn how to fold a tee. Readers who are parents of teenaged children might find that speed interesting. Toyota plans to deploy the bots alongside human workers in its own factories, where they will be free to move about using either a battery or an extension cord as an energy source. The company hopes its partners will also employ ELEY. India has five functional fabs The government of India last week announced that the nation is now home to five functioning semiconductor fabrication plants and said its latest industry promotion scheme has drawn $12 billion of investment. Minister for Electronics and Information Technology Ashwini Vaishnaw said India hopes to create “a complete semiconductor ecosystem” but offered no information about the nation’s attempts to create indigenous processors for local use. Vaishnaw last year said work is under way to produce a 7nm processor as part of India’s Shakti project, which aims to enable the country to produce its own servers and even supercomputers. Status updates on that effort are few and far between, and the project is yet to produce a modern microprocessor suitable for use in a personal device or server. ®

events.title: If your kid does these 8 things, they're more emotionally mature than most, says psychologist
events.summary: Raising Successful Kids Parents who are really good at handling tantrums do 5 things—their kids become more emotionally intelligent, says psychologist Raising Successful Kids Stop telling kids they can do anything—what parents can say instead to raise successful kids, says psychologist Psychology and Relationships The happiest couples do these 4 things early on—they've 'already built a roadmap,' says Harvard-trained psychologist Raising Successful Kids I’ve studied 200 kids: Parents whose kids still confide in them as adults do 7 things early on Psychology and Relationships I'm a psychologist who studies couples: 7 red flags of an 'extremely' unhealthy relationship How do you know if your child is showing healthy emotional development? As a clinical psychologist with over 30 years of experience and the author of "How to Raise an Emotionally Mature Child," I know it's when they are getting better at dealing with their feelings, other people and the outside world. An emotionally mature child will grow up to be a psychologically well-equipped adult who can handle the stresses of life on their own. They turn into adaptable, reasonable people who can solve problems, sustain satisfying long-term relationships and engage in meaningful work. Your patience, attention and affection now provide the essential support for a lifetime of resilience. Here are eight signs your child is emotionally mature (or maturing) — and how you can encourage and foster their emotional development and resilience. 1. They show vitality and involvement They're enthusiastic about their interests, their play is immersive and creative and they seek out positive experiences. This motivated energy can be exhausting for you as a parent, but it will sustain your kids' momentum in adult life. What you can do: You feed children's vitality when you listen to their ideas — regardless of whether you later give permission. So show them that they can share their ideas with you, and that you won't rain on their parade. 2. They increasingly show self-awareness and empathy As children mature, they develop a sense of self based on an awareness of inner experiences. This growing self-awareness soon translates into empathy for others and respecting others' points of view. What you can do: It's simple. Children learn to be interested in other people's feelings when you're interested in theirs. 3. They stand up for themselves but can be reasonable A successfully maturing child isn't afraid to stand up for themselves or tell you what they think. At the same time, if you offer some choice and explanation, they can collaborate and cooperate. What you can do: You teach your child to be their own person by honoring their right to speak up, even if you have no intention of changing your mind. You support their self-advocacy, but you also show them how to work things out respectfully when there's a disagreement. 4. They enjoy closeness and aren't afraid to be emotionally vulnerable Your emotionally maturing child feels safe showing you their vulnerable side. They see you as a person they can share their deeper feelings with. As long as you respect their autonomy and privacy, even teenagers will turn to you for affection and comfort. What you can do: You show your child how to enjoy emotional closeness in relationships when you take their feelings seriously and don't minimize or invalidate their experiences. 5. They're getting better at expressing and controlling their feelings As they mature, kids are better able to handle difficult feelings without falling apart or blaming others. Their tolerance for stress improves, and they gradually build a capacity for some patience. They know why they're upset and at whom but usually refrain from being mean or rude toward others. They own their feelings but are also learning that others will be affected by what they say and how they say it. They learn to object without attacking. What you can do: When you give kids confidence that you'll listen to their side of the story and understand their feelings, you minimize any need for them to act out or become passive aggressive. As a child becomes more of an individual, they follow their curiosity and like to learn and set goals for themselves. They might enjoy playing, making things, collecting things and planning projects. What you can do: If your child is thinking up ideas and coming to you with their grand schemes, you're probably doing a good job of mentoring their creativity and self-confidence. 7. They're adequately independent for their age And they experiment with their own ideas for solving problems. They aren't afraid to make mistakes in the process. What you can do: Even if they sometimes demand too much independence — which means you need to set limits — give yourself kudos for making them feel confident enough to go out in the world and take on challenges. 8.

events.title: Qatar’s energy chief sees LNG expansion start-up in 2027
events.summary: QatarEnergy’s liquefied natural gas production facilities in Ras Laffan Industrial City. Disruptions such as the Iran war have choked supplies of the fuel from Qatar, the world’s second-largest exporter. DOHA – Qatar expects inaugural output from its massive liquefied natural gas (LNG) expansion in 2027 as shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz slow projects across the country’s economy, Energy Minister Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi said. The first production train at North Field East – the initial phase of Qatar’s LNG expansion – is expected to come online in the first half of 2027, Al-Kaabi said at the Qatar Economic Forum in New York on Sept 20. The company previously anticipated that the plant would start producing in 2026. Bloomberg reported earlier in 2026 that the facility’s start had been delayed into 2027. Al-Kaabi warned that a prolonged disruption to Hormuz could delay some of its LNG expansion plans and the start of additional production trains. “ It will depend a lot on the Hormuz Strait for the additional trains that are going to come, because that could push it back if we can’t get facilities coming in,” he said. The North Field South project – the second phase of the project – is slated to come online in 2028, Al-Kaabi said. The timeline reinforces the expectations that the near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran war threatens to tighten global LNG supplies for years, as Qatar’s expansion was part of a record wave of new supply set to flood the market this decade. Disruptions have already choked supplies of the fuel from Qatar – the world’s second-largest exporter – sending spot prices surging to the highest level since 2022 in Asia and Europe. Still, Al-Kaabi said that Hormuz will never be obsolete, adding that US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is “wrong” when he said that the waterway will be worthless in two years. Al-Kaabi also said that Qatar is not currently planning to build new pipelines to bypass Hormuz. The disruption has sent shockwaves through Qatar’s economy, as natural gas revenue has all but evaporated and the country has no alternative shipping routes to bypass the strait. Qatar is expected to suffer an economic contraction of more than 8 per cent in 2026, according to the International Monetary Fund. Qatar’s Ras Laffan plant – which produced nearly a fifth of the world’s LNG before the war began in February – can resume operations at undamaged parts of the facility “within a couple of weeks” when Hormuz reopens, the minister said. An attack on Ras Laffan in the early days of the war – which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran – damaged about 17 per cent of the plant, which will take years to repair. Qatar is currently exporting a very small amount of LNG through the strait, Al-Kaabi said. The country is pivoting to become a larger trader of LNG, and is handling more LNG outside the Persian Gulf with the start of its Golden Pass export facility in the US. “We will be, in the very near future, the largest LNG trader in the world by far,” said Al-Kaabi. “And we’re building our position to become the largest trader.” Shell’s Pearl GTL facility in Qatar, which was also damaged in the March attacks, will resume production in the first quarter of 2027, he said. events.title: Incredible Holdings says independent director assisting in CAD, MAS investigation
events.summary: Incredible Holdings was told by Singapore Exchange Securities Trading that it was deemed a cash company with effect from May 28, as it no longer had any revenue-generating business. Incredible Holdings disclosed that an independent director is assisting the Commercial Affairs Department and Monetary Authority of Singapore in an investigation related to company affairs. The director attended an interview on Sept 18 about offences under the Securities and Futures Act, but no further details have been shared by authorities. The company’s shares have been suspended since Sept 2022, and it faces regulatory pressure to hold overdue meetings and update shareholders on future plans to avoid disciplinary actions. SINGAPORE – Catalist-listed Incredible Holdings has said that one of its independent directors is assisting in investigations by the Commercial Affairs Department (CAD) and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS). “The company understands from the independent director that the investigation is related to the affairs of the company,” it stated in a filing on the Singapore Exchange (SGX) website on Sept 19. The filing was made by Incredible’s board and its independent non-executive chairman Jacob Leung. It did not identify the independent director involved with the investigation. Incredible stated in its filing that the independent director received a letter dated Sept 17 from CAD and MAS, requiring them to attend an interview in relation to an investigation on offences under the Securities and Futures Act (Chapter 289) and Securities and Futures Act 2001. The independent director attended the interview on Sept 18 held by the CAD and MAS to assist in the investigation. “CAD and MAS have not given the company any further details of their investigations,” Incredible said. The minutes of an information session held by the company on Aug 27 and filed with SGX on Sept 8 listed Eunice Koh as an independent director who attended the session along with Leung, who is also an independent director. The minutes said that Zhou Jia Lin, a non-executive non-independent director, had sent her apologies for not being able to attend the information session. Also unable to attend was Phillip Fei, who was appointed executive director in July, as he was in Beijing at the time of the meeting. Incredible’s shares have been suspended since September 2022. It held its last annual general meeting (AGM) on Aug 15, 2023 and has not convened meetings for the financial periods ended June 2024 and June 2025 , placing it in breach of listing rules. As a result, Incredible was directed by the Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo), in a notice of compliance dated April 28, to hold an in-person information session within four months to update shareholders on the company’s state of affairs and future plans, and to give investors an opportunity to raise concerns. Incredible was told that it was expected to convene all outstanding AGMs within one year. Failure to comply with these directives could result in disciplinary action, including placing directors and executives on a watch-list, SGX RegCo said. In late May, Incredible Holdings was notified by Singapore Exchange Securities Trading that it was deemed a cash company under Rule 1017(1) of Catalist Rules with effect from May 28, as the company no longer had any revenue-generating business. events.title: Macron backs Canada as EU associate member as Carney turns toward Europe
events.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron has backed a proposal for Canada to become the European Union’s first associate member as he and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney deepen ties in space, defense, energy and business TORONTO -- French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday backed a proposal for Canada to become the European Union’s first associate member as he and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney moved to deepen strategic ties spanning space, defense, energy and business. The leaders met in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, a French territory just off Newfoundland’s coast where France and Canada are separated by only a few kilometers (miles) — a striking setting for Canada’s accelerating turn toward Europe as relations with the United States deteriorate. “We are very much in favor of that agenda of closer ties with the European Union, as an associate member of the Union, as the president said, and as a full-fledged member of the European community,” Macron said in French while standing alongside Carney. “Only a few kilometers separate Canada and France at their closest point. Our values are even closer,” Carney said in French. Carney said the countries will task their space agencies and defense ministries to develop and share infrastructure, including launch systems and ground-based reception facilities. They also agreed to expand cooperation in energy, telecommunications, climate resilience and economic development. Macron’s endorsement comes days after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada the EU’s first associate member . Carney embraced the prospect and has argued that deeper ties with Europe would give Canada more alternatives and make it less vulnerable to economic coercion by any single country. Trump’s tariffs , demands for economic concessions and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st U.S. state have accelerated that turn toward Europe. Trump also recently posted a map on social media draping the U.S. flag across all of North America, including Canada and Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon. Macron welcomed Carney on Sunday at the airport in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, the French territory of about 5,800 people just off Newfoundland’s coast. Macron also said that Sunday’s talks are part of broader efforts to help France secure oil and gas supplies as the Iran war disrupts global energy markets and raises fears of higher prices for fuel and other essentials. “Canada is a country with significant resources of critical minerals and rare earths. It is also a major oil and natural gas producer,” Macron said. “What we want to do is conclude agreements to secure more liquefied natural gas that can be shipped to Europe’s Atlantic coast.” Cindy Crawford's son Presley Gerber dies at 27 Protesters form human chain at Kennedy Center amid Trump's threats to demolish it Twin sisters conjoined at head underwent successful separation surgery: Hospital The leaders discussed aerospace, energy, critical minerals and advanced technologies such as quantum computing, satellites and supercomputing, Carney’s office said in a statement. Carney returned to Ottawa later Sunday to meet Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre for talks on defense, Arctic security, energy, critical minerals and emerging technologies before heading to New York on Monday for the U.N. General Assembly. At a joint news conference with Støre, Carney rejected the idea that deeper ties with European allies should be seen as hostile to the United States, saying Canada is a better partner when it is “more independent or more resilient” and has stronger relationships around the world. Sunday’s meeting also follows Trump’s announcement of a deal on Greenland that would expand the U.S. military presence there while keeping the island under Danish control. The agreement followed months of threats by Trump to seize the semiautonomous territory of a NATO ally . events.title: Inside the 24 hours that laid bare Tata’s brutal power struggle
events.summary: Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran, known as Chandra, had helmed the closely held company for a decade, and had signalled openness to the idea of taking it public. Tata Sons' board extended chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran's term despite opposition from Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata, deepening a power struggle over the conglomerate's future and public listing plans. Noel Tata argued to keep Tata Sons private, proposing alternatives like share buybacks to avoid listing, but the board voted 4-1 to comply with regulatory demands to list shares. The conflict sparked public confrontations, legal threats, and market volatility, highlighting internal divisions amid Tata Group's critical projects and leadership uncertainty. Shortly before noon on Sept 17, the directors of Tata Sons, the holding company for India’s biggest conglomerate, gathered for a meeting in a sleek boardroom on the fourth floor of its headquarters. On one side of the long table that can accommodate 20 people sat Noel Tata, chairman of Tata Trusts. The group of charities owns 66 per cent of a holding company that in turn controls some of India’s biggest brand names from Air India to Jaguar Land Rover. Sleeves rolled up, a seven-page document at the ready, he came prepared with a strategy to keep the company that carries his family name in private hands. Among those facing him was Natarajan Chandrasekaran, chairman of Tata Sons, wearing a suit and a fuchsia tie. Chandrasekaran, known as Chandra, had helmed the closely held company for a decade, and had signalled openness to the idea of taking it public. But after his reappointment failed to secure unanimity earlier in 2026, he decided to bow out instead of seeking another term. Yet, it was not Chandra’s last act. In a surprise move, Tata Sons’ directors voted 4-1 to extend his tenure for another five years and planned to move forward with steps toward a public listing – rebuffing Noel’s position and deepening a rift over control and the future of the 158-year-old conglomerate. Tata Sons’ directors voted to extend chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran’s tenure for another 5=five years. The split has set off a civil war that is likely to reach India’s courts and Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government before it can be resolved. A stark battle line has been drawn, with Tata Sons describing matters as settled and Tata Trusts calling the vote to extend Chandra’s term “illegal”. The controversy over Tata Sons and its chairman’s tenure is set to fuel uncertainty about the Indian conglomerate’s leadership at a time when it is helming several prestige projects for India. Tata Group has plans to expand local production of Apple iPhones, and is building India’s first chipmaking facility. The group’s existing businesses are among the country’s most pervasive and renowned, including global brands like Taj Hotels, consumer staples such as Tetley tea and software giant Tata Consultancy Services. Tension among directors had been building even before anyone arrived for the meeting at Bombay House, the group’s headquarters in Mumbai. The immediate chain of events began on Sept 11, when India’s central bank rejected a petition by Tata Sons to exempt it from a regulatory path that would require a public listing. The day before the board convened, one of the trusts sought – unsuccessfully – to prevent its representative director, Venu Srinivasan, from attending the meeting and voting on the board proposals, reflecting internal schisms that would soon burst into public view. This account of the 24 hours surrounding the meeting is based on interviews with people familiar with the events, who asked not to be identified because the discussions were private. Representatives for Tata Trusts and Tata Sons did not respond to requests for comment. Srinivasan did not immediately respond to a request for comment. For the first half hour of the pivotal meeting, board members talked about normal business affairs such as quarterly performance and accounts, the people familiar said. Then the discussion turned to the decision by the Reserve Bank of India and the mood shifted as the gravity of the subject matter weighed on those in attendance, the people said. Noel argued a listing was not inevitable, methodically explaining why that position could be defended, without raising his voice or displaying any hint of hostile body language, according to people familiar with the meeting. His proposal was for the board to ask Tata Sons to go back to the regulator, seek a hearing with top officials to plead its case and then exhaust all other legal options to remain private. If those efforts failed, he said the company could seek at least three more years to comply, arguing that a listing would require extensive corporate approvals and financial preparation. The fate of Tata Sons’ structure as a closely held entity is intertwined with the death of Ratan Tata, the group’s former patriarch and Noel’s half-brother, in October 2024.

events.title: New 'blanket' Safe Work rules not practical, say miners and farmers
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Farmers and miners say new dust and chemical restrictions may be impossible to measure Acceptable limits of grain dust exposure have been slashed, but farmers say they need help measuring and complying with new standards. ( ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Jo Prendergast ) New rules for workplace exposure to dust, chemicals and gasses come into effect on December 1, but mine and farm groups say they are not practical or measurable. Safe Work Australia formed the new rules, but enforcing the limits will be up to each state. Industry groups are lobbying government to consider changing or delaying the rollout. Farmers and miners in Western Australia are nervous about new workplace safety rules that will reduce accepted exposure levels of dust and certain chemicals from December 1. New rules set by Safe Work Australia (SWA) will reduce the safe exposure limit for hundreds of dusts, fumes and chemicals found in Australian workplaces. The change is designed to protect workers, but industry groups say some new limits are so low there is no practical way to measure them. Farming groups are warning the new rules could disrupt grain harvest and are calling on the government to intervene. Most grain storage in Australia relies on phosphine to keep out insects. ( ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Jo Prendergast ) West Australian Grain Group chair Alastair Falconer said farmers were alarmed SWA's accepted exposure limit for the fumigant phosphine will be slashed by 80 per cent. Mr Falconer said the grain industry relied on phosphine to keep insects out of stored or exported grain, but said the new rule "almost renders phosphine unusable". Exports play a big role in Australia's $33 billion grain industry, but many importing countries will reject entire shipments if insects are found due to biosecurity laws. Mr Falconer said the new exposure limits for grain dust, including oats, wheat and barley had been more than halved. He said the industry was scrambling to find information on how to measure grain dust exposure, and how to comply with the new regulations. "To be honest, I wasn't aware of what our grain dust limits were until now," he said. "When we're blowing down harvesters, we're cleaning out our own silos, what exposure is that giving us, how do you measure exposure when you're blowing down a harvester, and what's the correct PPE to use to make sure you don't go over this new limit. "I think we need a three-year delay on implementing [the new rules] while industry can do more research on are these levels appropriate, or how we manage them into the future?" Grain dust is an inevitable part of harvest operations. ( ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Jo Prendergast ) In a statement, Safe Work Australia said workplace exposure limits were used to protect workers and the revised workplace exposure limits reflect current scientific evidence and independent expert advice. Safe Work said it conducted public consultation in 2019-2021, and the new limits were agreed by work health and safety ministers and published in April 2024 for implementation on December 1, 2026. "Safe Work Australia recognises there are questions about how limits for phosphine and other airborne contaminants are applied in practice and is working with industry stakeholders and other government agencies, including the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority and the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, to support a consistent understanding of the requirements," the statement said. "Compliance is assessed through personal air monitoring of workers, rather than measuring levels of an airborne contaminant at a fixed location." Safe Work pointed to more information on its website. The new standards are set by Safe Work Australia, but will be implemented by states legislation. In August, WorkSafe Victoria said it would delay workplace exposure limits for 15 airborne contaminants, including phosphine, until December 1, 2029. Grain industry groups met with West Australian Agriculture Minister Jackie Jarvis last week raising concerns about phosphine and grain dust compliance. New Safe Work rules slash acceptable exposure to manganese dust. ( Supplied ) The minister told the ABC she was seeking more information from the impact of the new phosphine limits on the grains industry. More than 600 substances are covered by the new workplace exposure limit (WEL) system, with exposure limits tightened for about 250 of them. The WEL defines the maximum level of airborne contaminant that most people can be exposed to without harming their health.

events.title: I felt confident in my appearance and how I dressed. Then, I moved to Japan.
events.summary: I didn't realize how much moving to Japan would change how I view my body and make me so critical of how I dress. Kerri King Moving to Japan made me more self-conscious about my appearance than I've ever been before. Being noticeably different from those around me made me critical of my body and how I dress. On the bright side, living here pushed me to explore beauty, style, and self-expression in new ways. Moving to a new country comes with plenty of adjustments, from language to social rules, but I didn't expect to feel out of place in my own body. Before moving to Japan from New Zealand, I was mostly content with how I looked, having already survived the body-image hurdles of early motherhood. Despite being a plus-size woman , I considered myself to be confident and rarely cared what others thought of my appearance. After three years here, the visibility that comes with being a foreigner has brought along a level of self-consciousness I have never grappled with before. I couldn't stop comparing myself to everyone around me Wherever I went, I felt like I was being judged even if I wasn't. IronHeart/Getty Images Being visibly non-Japanese meant I often felt more conspicuous than I ever had, and that made me hyper-aware of how I looked. I often felt like people were staring at me, making me wonder what they were noticing, and before long, I found I was scrutinizing parts of myself I hadn't thought about before. The hair on my arms used to feel as normal as having eyebrows, but after noticing how uncommon visible body hair seemed to be among locals, I became convinced I must look like a yeti in comparison, and soon found myself reaching for a razor. Still, I always thought a bit of body hair never hurt anyone until an older woman, who had been openly staring at my legs, scoffed as she walked past and shook her head. Afterward, I found myself questioning whether it was my slightly unshaven legs or the large tattoo on my calf that had prompted such a reaction. Tattoos in Japan can feel taboo, as they carry a long-standing association with the country's organized crime groups. Many bathhouses, swimming pools, gyms, and other public facilities still restrict access for people with tattoos. Whatever the reason, I spent the rest of the day acutely aware of my body and still think about that moment whenever I put on a pair of shorts. It can be tough to get used to the style and trends in a new place. KAZUHIRO NOGI/AFP via Getty Images Shopping for clothes here hasn't exactly helped me build confidence either. Back home, I typically wear a US size 16 to 18. In Japan, that generally puts me at around a 3L or 4L, sizes I've mostly only found at select stores or through online retailers. Much of the mainstream clothing here seems to cater to the smaller, more petite proportions common in the Japanese market, leaving fewer options for bodies like mine. The experience of repeatedly trying on clothes that don't fit the way I expect can turn into self-loathing. Instead of thinking that the clothes simply aren't designed with my proportions in mind, I find myself questioning my body. In time, I started changing my style to fit in As a teenager, I went through different phases with my hair color. Courtesy of Kerri King Growing up in rural New Zealand never demanded much in the way of fashion or beauty. It felt perfectly acceptable to pop into the supermarket wearing sweatpants and gumboots (rubber rain boots), or even go barefoot. For most of my life, my style barely changed . My hair has cycled through every color imaginable, and about 90% of my wardrobe has come from the same label: Drop Dead Clothing, an alternative, grungy brand. I rarely wore makeup, and my skincare routine consisted of little more than face wash, moisturizer, and sunscreen in summer. Looking back at old photos, it's obvious I never put much energy into fitting conventional beauty standards . Beauty culture often felt like another set of expectations largely placed on women, and I viewed much of it with a healthy dose of skepticism. I've found myself buying more beauty products than I used to. Bloomberg/Getty Images Moving to Japan quickly challenged that perspective. I became much more aware of the country's beauty culture , from the sheer number of skincare and makeup products available in stores to the constant stream of J-beauty hauls and "must-try" products appearing on my Instagram feed. I also noticed how put-together people often looked in everyday settings. While sweatpants and a slightly disheveled look had always been perfectly acceptable for a quick supermarket run back home, I rarely saw adults dressed that casually here. Surrounded by those trends and expectations, I found myself questioning choices I had worn confidently for years. Although I still dye my hair and hold on to parts of the aesthetic I've had since my teens, I haven't owned a pair of gumboots since moving here. I also catch myself second-guessing my outfit before a basic run to the convenience store. I know that, as a foreigner living in Japan , I will never completely "fit in," but I actively try to avoid the attention that comes with looking out of place. Bit by bit, comfort has lost ground to conformity. I wear makeup more frequently and have built a collection of viral Japanese beauty products that my younger self would have scoffed at. Living in Japan changed how I see myself — and pushed me to explore my identity I'm grateful that living in Japan has pushed me to experiment with my self-expression. Zhang Peng/LightRocket via Getty Images I don't like that I've become more self-conscious, but I've also realized that how we present ourselves isn't always about meeting external expectations. It can also be shaped by habit and exposure to different norms. Some of the changes I have made to my appearance have come from insecurity — others from curiosity — and I still haven't fully untangled where one ends and the other begins. At the same time, I'm grateful for how living in Japan has pushed me to experiment with forms of self-expression I would have dismissed outright a few years ago. I've enjoyed exploring makeup and a more feminine side of my style, from accessorizing with cute hair clips and handbags to building a surprisingly nice shoe collection now that my beloved gumboots are no longer an option. It has forced me to question how much of my self-image is truly mine, and how much has been shaped by the places and expectations around me. As uncomfortable as that process has sometimes been, it has also shown me that personal growth and insecurity are not always separate things. Sometimes they arrive together. events.title: Exclusive: Beshear says next president must go big on housing
events.summary: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear signaled in an interview with Axios that he would put America's housing affordability crisis at the center of his campaign if he ran for president in 2028. Why it matters: It's the latest sign that Beshear, who just kicked off a national book tour, is moving closer to a bid for the White House. Driving the news: Beshear said the next president should pursue a massive housing initiative — with strict guidelines to ensure the money is spent quickly. "There's a chance for the next presidential administration or the next Congress to make a big, bold investment in housing that could have us building millions of units all over the United States," he said. "We cannot do this in drips and drabs. It can't be mild investments over a period of time." Echoing the "Abundance" movement, which calls for slashing regulations in order to lower housing costs, Beshear said federal dollars sent to states should be used quickly or withdrawn. "If you tie the federal dollars to that timing, you will break through the regulation and the NIMBYism," he said. Beshear declined to put a specific price tag on his vision, saying that those details could be discussed with lawmakers. But he said $150 billion in federal spending could theoretically lead to $1 trillion of housing being built if enough outside financing were leveraged. By the numbers: Escalating home prices have become a major political issue in recent years. Sixty-four percent of American adults say they're "very concerned" about the cost of housing, according to a Pew Research Center poll in July. The intrigue: After talking policy, we asked Beshear about rumors swirling in Democratic circles that he could announce a run for president as soon as December. "I would tell you that that is solely a rumor," he said of the winter timeline. "I haven't made any final decisions yet." But, sounding as if he's close to making up his mind, Beshear added, "Listen, I don't want to leave a broken country to my kids."

events.title: Many ex-aides to Harris betting against a 2028 run
events.summary: Many of those who know Kamala Harris best think she ultimately won't run for the White House in 2028. Why it matters: What the former vice president decides to do is one of the biggest X factors in the next presidential contest: Early polls suggest Harris is the frontrunner to be the Democratic nominee, and if she opted out, it would scramble the primary. Zoom in: Over the past year, a surprisingly large number of former aides, surrogates and donors to Harris have told Axios they believe she won't launch another campaign. They argue that the moves she's making — hitting the trail for midterm candidates, going on the podcast circuit, and writing a book — might make her look like a contender-in-waiting, but actually amount to her simply trying to maintain influence. Harris has said publicly and privately she hasn't made up her mind yet, and some of her former aides concede they could be wrong — or could even be "wishcasting" because they don't want her to pursue another bid. This week, we surveyed eight former Harris aides and advisers, including those who worked for her at a senior level, to get their most up-to-date read. Only one thought Harris probably will run. Two said it's a coin-flip, and five said she likely won't. Here's why: She's doing "the bare minimum" to stay in the 2028 conversation, as one past aide put it. Harris' former staffers argue that if she were gung-ho about running she'd be hiring more, traveling more, and inserting herself into policy debates more often. She's a rational actor. Former aides say Harris is well aware of the hurdles that would await her if she ran again. "She's a realist and an astute political observer, and she knows her candidacy could get bogged down in a 2024 rearview mirror," said a second former aide. The money might not be there. Many high-dollar donors are still furious about Harris' loss and don't want her to run again. Top Democratic donor Reid Hoffman said last week that she'd face "a very challenging path" in 2028. Some of her former financial backers are signaling support for other potential candidates, such as Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and California Gov. Gavin Newsom . She isn't an egomaniac. Sure, this is self-serving. But multiple people who worked for Harris say she lacks the "sociopathic" belief — their words, not ours — that it's she and she alone who should be president. Some tea leaves suggest she's lukewarm on running . Harris effectively gave up control of her @KamalaHQ social media account, and bought an $8 million house in Malibu with her husband. Also, her top aide Kirsten Allen left her team recently, though Harris still speaks with her. What they're saying: A former Harris aide connected to Axios by her current team put the odds of another run at "50-50," saying the former VP "is a very methodical decision-maker" who will weigh "the moment that we're in." This former aide pushed back on the notion that money could be a problem, pointing to Harris' massive email fundraising list and arguing that high-dollar donors won't determine the next nominee. They also said her team doesn't need to be bigger when the focus is on the midterms. "There will be a lot of people who will feel a lot of urgency to announce as soon as possible," the former aide said. "I think the vice president doesn't necessarily have to be on that timeline." The lone former Harris staffer who told us they expect her to run gave it a "55% chance," noting that Harris has been ramping up her calls to Democratic officials and activists. "I think there's a lot of wishcasting that maybe Kamala will come to her senses and not do it," this person said. Harris definitely is keeping the door open to another bid, including by gearing up to campaign this fall for battleground candidates such as Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and Nevada gubernatorial hopeful Aaron Ford. But many former aides who think Harris would be a good president say they don't want her to run again because they seriously doubt she could win, given her record. One way to view their arguments: They're trying to persuade her to stay out of the race. David Plouffe, Harris' 2024 senior adviser, was blunt about the headwinds she would face in a third national campaign, even as he acknowledged she'd begin in an enviable position. " Her strongest day will be her first day in the campaign," Plouffe told "Pod Save America," predicting Harris' support likely would erode as the race developed. The bottom line: People who talk to Harris say she's genuinely undecided about 2028, but political insiders will keep scrutinizing her every move for signs of what she'll do next. During a recent podcast interview , she told former soccer star Megan Rapinoe: "I don't know how to live and not serve." Axios' Alex Thompson contributed to this report.

events.title: With this 'little bit', households can help tackle organic waste problem
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Home composting championed as fix to growing burden of organic waste in landfill Topic: Recycling and Waste Management Benjamin Head believes residents can go a long way to help with landfill diversion by recycling. ( ABC News: Michael Lloyd ) Diverting waste from landfill is an increasing priority across the country. The Queensland government wants to recycle 65 per cent of the state's waste by 2035. Addressing food and garden waste is key but a lack of green and FOGO bin services has brought home recycling and composting into focus. Every drop makes an ocean is a motto sustainable-living champion Benjamin Head wants everyone to be guided by. From food scraps and garden clippings to paper, cardboard, old bottle caps and packaging material, the 62-year-old puts to use materials many of us throw out as general rubbish. Over more than two decades, Mr Head has made his suburban home on the Gold Coast a waste ecosystem of its own and has seen his rubbish pile progressively shrink. Queensland lagging behind organic waste goals Green food and garden organic bins — known as FOGO bins — have been heralded as the answer to diverting organic materials away from landfill, but Queensland is falling behind on its goals. "It's gradually getting less and less," he said. "I get a bit more money in my pocket and we leave the Gold Coast in a better place for our future generations. "Think before you toss. Look in the bin and see if there's anything of value and pull that out, it doesn't take very long, and put that into a separate bin or bucket." Mr Head said his farming background gave him a head start with integrating the circular-economy model into his daily life, but recycling habits could be adopted by anybody, and on any scale. His process is simple: most leftovers from the kitchen table and cooking go into a large backyard composting bin and some to feed the chickens. Benjamin Head is passionate about educating people on how to compost and recycle better at home. ( ABC News: Michael Lloyd ) Cane mulch, grass clippings, flowers and leaves are added to the composting mix, along with shreds of paper and cardboard. The product is a nutrient-rich soil, which Mr Head puts back into the garden to grow a variety of fresh organic fruit and vegetables, saving money on the grocery shop. "We have 300,000 tonnes of [residual] waste [annually] in the Gold Coast; we have 680,000 people," he said. "If we can get everybody to do a little bit, then we're heading in the right direction." What Mr Head does forms part of a much larger goal by government to reduce the amount of waste sent to landfill and to improve recycling rates. Queensland's latest waste strategy , released in June, sets a target of reducing residual waste, collected from statewide red bins, by 65 per cent in the next decade. Addressing food and garden waste is a top priority under the plan. Half of the state's total landfill waste comprises organics, which, upon decomposing, produce the dangerous greenhouse gas methane. Organic waste makes up 50 per cent of what goes into red rubbish bins across Queensland each year. ( ABC News: Michael Lloyd ) However, just 11 of Queensland's 77 councils provide a kerbside green bin service for garden waste and only some provide FOGO bins for food and organic waste, by request. These are concentrated in the state's south-east. It is also in this region where the strategy has set the biggest landfill-reduction target of 70 per cent over 10 years. Council-led initiatives, such as the Advanced Resource Recovery Centre (ARRC) on the Gold Coast, have introduced programs incentivising residential organic recycling . "That's an opportunity for residents of the Gold Coast to get low-cost home composting and worm farms available," ARRC CEO Grant Gabriel said. "It's important that all Australians think about what goes into your green bin and, if any of that can be turned into home composting to make their gardens more healthy, where they're growing roses or fruit out of there, there's an opportunity for everyone to really bring that circularity into their home." Grant Gabriel says resource recovery is equally about the role of households, developing the end market for recycled goods, and landfill alternatives. ( ABC News: Michael Lloyd ) The waste strategy also recognises the need to provide additional funding for organics-processing infrastructure, including green bins, and support for activities such as home composting and community composting.

events.title: Betting on People-First Banking
events.summary: China CITIC Bank International’s Wendy Yuen says the future of finance will not be won by technology alone, but by banks that combine digital speed with human trust, cross-border insight and lifelong learning. As head of the Personal and Business Banking Group at China CITIC Bank International, Wendy Yuen sits at the intersection of technology, regulation and real-world customer needs. Based in Hong Kong, she works across retail banking, SME support, fintech innovation and cross-border growth in the Greater Bay Area. Across that wide remit, her message is consistent: technology is powerful, but people and purpose must come first. “We are a society of people,” she says, “particularly in the banking industry, the service industry. We are using people to serve people.” For Yuen, the most profound change in banking is not digitalisation itself, but what it allows banks to become. The old advantage of a large branch network is giving way to a model built on speed, convenience and intelligent connectivity. In the past, she says, a major bank’s strength came from having “the most extensive network” and “the most people”. Today, success is no longer only about physical reach. It is about “how fast we get in touch with you, and how we make your life convenient”. She argues that digitalisation still has limits, especially when customers are making decisions about money, family and long-term security. “Digitisation gives you timeliness and convenience,” she says, particularly for standardised and commoditised services. “But for complicated matters, customers still want a professional.” This is why she notes the importance of a hybrid model in which technology handles basic tasks while people focus on high-trust conversations: mortgages, holistic investment planning, legacy arrangements and business growth. “Technology simply replaces some very basic things,” she says, helping customers and bank staff work more efficiently. The same philosophy applies to trust. Even in highly digital markets, Yuen notes that some technology companies have embraced offline contact because customers still want to see, touch and feel before making certain decisions. That contact, she says, “builds the credibility and it builds the trust”, even when the final transaction is completed through technology. Inside the bank, she has pushed for collaboration across business lines, from investment banking and asset management to trust, securities and retail banking. The aim is to serve the customer as a whole person, rather than as a set of disconnected accounts. “We serve one person, his family, the corporation, and ultimately the whole society,” she says. In an industry often organised around silos and products, Yuen is organising banking around the customer’s life journey instead. Indeed, Yuen’s forward-looking agenda is anchored in three forces: fintech, the Greater Bay Area and data-driven personalisation. Customers no longer compare banks with other banks. They compare them with every digital service in their lives. “Customers today have higher expectations,” she says. “It’s 24x7.” That reality has led China CITIC Bank International to adopt a mobile-first strategy, with more than 80 per cent of the bank’s banking transactions coming through mobile channels. “You can lose your wallet, but you cannot lose your mobile phone today,” she says. “Because everything is on that.” For her, this is a response to how people live, work and move, particularly in the fast-paced Greater Bay Area (GBA) in southern China. The GBA is central to her view of the future. Yuen sees Hong Kong as both gateway and platform: international enough to connect businesses and investors with the world, and close enough to the mainland to understand the region’s growth, capital and wealth-management needs. Her focus now stretches from individuals moving to Hong Kong under talent and residency schemes to SMEs and large corporations using the city as a launchpad. “If you want to get access to the world, the first office could be in Hong Kong,” she says. “We can help them to land and then push further out.” Another pillar is the internationalisation of the renminbi. Yuen sees Hong Kong as a leading offshore RMB centre, with growing relevance as companies seek funding, products and settlement solutions linked to the currency. “Hong Kong is a very good platform,” she says. “If you want to get access to RMB, Hong Kong is getting more and more exciting in this arena.” For SMEs, she believes the next five years will be defined by cross-border and multi-market business. Banks will need to provide payment gateways, digitalisation tools and cross-border solutions that allow smaller firms to operate beyond their home markets. “As the world is more connected,” she says, “it’s actually the cross-border payment solution, digitalisation solution, the payment gateway, staying connected at every portal, that helps a company or SME do business.

events.title: askST Jobs: How to tell if you’re being micromanaged or closely supervised. What’s the difference?
events.summary: There is a difference between a boss who checks in on employees and one who constantly hovers like a “helicopter parent” over them. In this series, business correspondent Timothy Goh offers practical answers to candid questions on navigating workplace challenges and getting ahead in your career. Get more tips by signing up to The Straits Times’ Headstart newsletter . How can I tell the difference between close supervision and micromanagement? Is it possible to ask for more autonomy without damaging my relationship with my manager? Employees should look at what their boss is actually doing and how the behaviour is affecting them, said counselling psychologist Padma Jairam. Some signs of micromanagement include having to provide excessive updates, needing a manager’s approval for even small and routine decisions, and having work repeatedly rewritten or heavily edited without a clear explanation. Micromanagers may also focus excessively on how work is done rather than the outcome. “Employees may also catch themselves overthinking routine decisions because they are preparing for someone to question them,” said Padma. But close supervision does not necessarily mean a manager thinks an employee is incapable of doing his or her job. “Often, it could be about your boss’ own anxiety or fears. They could be worried about being blindsided or getting blamed for a team member’s mistake,” she said. “Such behaviour could stem from a manager’s own anxieties or previous unpleasant experiences.” Although this does not justify micromanagement, understanding what may be driving the behaviour could help employees respond without becoming defensive. Padma said employees who interpret their boss’ behaviour as a sign of their own incompetence may become more anxious and, consequently, could make careless errors, which could give the manager even more reason to micromanage. “It’s a loop that worsens the situation for both the employee and the boss,” she said. “Understanding the so-called hovering as perhaps your boss’ own stress response, rather than a verdict on you, makes it a lot easier to respond calmly instead of getting defensive.” To regain some autonomy, employees could start by communicating proactively, such as providing a brief update before their manager asks for one. This could reassure the manager that a project is under control while giving the employee more space to get the work done. Employees should also clarify expectations at the beginning of a project, including what a successful outcome looks like and how frequently their manager expects updates. Trust may also have to be built gradually, said Padma. Employees could demonstrate their reliability on smaller tasks before seeking greater autonomy over more significant pieces of work. If a manager continues to demand more updates than necessary, employees could try negotiating rather than confronting them. Employees should also “pick their battles”, as they may not need complete independence on every task. “It is easier to accept more oversight on high-stakes projects while negotiating for more freedom on lower-risk ones,” Padma said. However, better communication may not resolve every case of micromanagement. “If the boss’ behaviour feels punitive and is ruining your sleep or your confidence, or if nothing changes, no matter what you try, then that may not be something you can fix with better communication,” she said. In such situations, employees could consider approaching the human resources department, a mentor or a senior colleague whom they trust for help. “Reaching out for help is not a sign of weakness but recognising that the problem is bigger than you,” said Padma. “Micromanagement can be annoying, but the good news is that it usually does not last forever... Most bosses ease up once they trust the outcome, and most people get that trust back faster than they expect once they stop taking the scrutiny personally and start treating it as something to work through.” David Leong, managing director of PeopleWorldwide Consulting, said employees should not immediately assume that close supervision means their manager is a micromanager. “Before labelling a boss a micromanager, ask yourself an uncomfortable question: Is the manager controlling by nature and always like that, or has something happened that caused the manager to lose confidence in me? Have I failed in meeting my goals and key performance indicators?” he said. Where trust has been affected, employees may be able to regain some autonomy by demonstrating that they can be relied upon to deliver their work. “Autonomy is rarely won through confrontation and assurances. It is usually earned through predictability and performance,” said Leong. When managers know that an employee delivers what they promise, flags problems early and does not create unpleasant surprises, their perceived need to closely monitor the employee should gradually diminish, he said.

events.title: World model companies are keeping a lot of secrets
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt This week, I moderated a panel on world models at the All In conference (no relation to the podcast), and it gave me a chance to dig into one of the most mysterious corners of the AI world. The big players in the space are Yann LeCun’s AMI Labs and Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs — and while both have accumulated a lot of buzz and funding, they also rank pretty low on the trying-to-make-money scale . At their core, world models are about automating spatial intelligence , so the field could head in lots of exciting and lucrative directions, from robotics to interactive video to more complex self-driving systems. But when I started to press on where we would actually see the tech commercialized, things got foggy. The closest thing I found to an authority was Michael Rabbat, a co-founder of AMI Labs and the company’s VP of World Models, who joined me on the panel. But when I pressed him on exactly what the company was working on, he was cagey. “We’ll talk about it when we’re ready to talk about it.” Over email, he clarified, “We’re still in a research and building phase, so we’re not talking publicly about any product plans or timeline.” To be fair, AMI is less than a year old, so it’s fair enough to keep quiet. But this sort of caginess extends to the whole world-modeling space. World Labs’ Marble is probably the most fully developed product in the space, and its demos range from straightforward media creation, building explorable environments for video games, or CGI effects. There are robotics use cases too, but the whole platform seems more designed to demonstrate capabilities. That secrecy even extends to these companies’ suppliers. On the sidelines of the same conference, I spoke to Alex de Vigan, CEO of Physicl — a data supplier for the burgeoning world model business. He says he knows Physicl’s data has been useful for whatever they’re building, but he’s still in the dark about what exactly that is. “I wish they would tell us more. We could build more useful data if we knew what they were working on,” de Vigan told me. Part of the mystery comes from how versatile world models are as an idea. The simplest version is a navigable map of the world, similar to the AI models that power self-driving cars. But the same modeling approach that helps a Waymo weave through traffic could also help a humanoid robot carry boxes, or turn a few minutes of video footage into an explorable environment. AMI has already dipped its toe in manufacturing, biomedicine, robotics, and even AI software for doctors through its Nabia partnership. Surely it won’t pursue all of those — but maybe one or two of them are standing out? No one doubts that there are lots of viable businesses to be built on world model tech — and as long as it’s easy to fundraise, there’s no particular pressure to focus on one. In fact, there’s good reason not to. If AMI announced tomorrow that they had built a humanoid OpenClaw or a next-generation Hollywood rendering system, a lot of other labs would suddenly be very interested in the space. Soon, the lab would face potential competition from the other world model companies, the neolabs, and even OpenAI and Anthropic. In some ways, it’s the flip side of all that easy fundraising. Your competitors can fundraise, too — and the same money that lets you build under the radar is also funding lots of potential rivals once the path to market becomes clear. But even if that competition is inevitable, it’s best if you delay it for as long as possible, which means keeping quiet about exactly what you’re building. Cixin Liu fans will recognize this as a dark forest scenario : If you don’t know who else is in the woods, it’s best not to attract attention. This post was first published on September 18, 2026. events.title: Concerns raised over Qld's call-in process for assessing renewable projects
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Renewable energy advocates say Qld's call-in process creates uncertainty for investors, communities The Queensland government is assessing several wind turbine proposals. ( ABC News: Nathan Morris ) Renewable energy advocates are calling for a better framework for development processes to ensure investors are not scared off. The Queensland government is using extraordinary powers to call in energy projects, leaving both communities and investors uncertain about the future. The Queensland government says its committed to energy projects, and has more under construction or financially promised than anywhere else in the country. Renewable energy advocates say increased government intervention in wind farms projects could threaten private sector investment as Queensland works out how to best support the growth of data centres in Australia. The Queensland government is in the process of using special "call-in" powers to assess at least three renewable energy projects across the state, after cancelling the Moonlight Range Wind Farm in Central Queensland in May 2025. The call-in powers are used during exceptional circumstances where Deputy Premier and Planning Minister Jarrod Bleije believes the project needs further assessment to ensure it meets economic and environmental state interests. The projects being assessed are the Bouldercombe Battery Energy Storage System near Rockhampton and two proposed projects on the Western Downs: the Marmadua Energy Park and the Middle Creek Energy Hub. The Western Downs projects are in the same region as the proposed $32 billion data centre, the Western Downs Digital Park, near the town of Dalby, about four hours' drive west of Brisbane. The concept model of a large-scale data centre project that has been proposed for the Western Downs. ( Supplied: Urbis ) Local federal member and Nationals MP David Littleproud has also called on the Queensland government to intervene in the federally approved $1.5 billion Tarong West Wind Farm proposed further north in the South Burnett region. This has raised concern in the Renewable Energy Alliance. National director Andrew Bray said the state government's enthusiasm for the exceptional powers could be a roadblock for investment in energy projects. Mr Bray, whose organisation advocates for the use of renewable energy to strengthen regional areas, said communities were calling for more clarity about the approval of projects and said call-ins could cloud that process. "Once a planning approval is given, then let's go ahead with it. If it's not, then we can move on to something else," he said. Andrew Bray says both regional communities and investors simply want clarity when it comes to the approval process for wide scale energy projects. ( Picture: ABC Southern Qld/Aisling Brennan ) Mr Littleproud said while he was "not against renewables", the Tarong West Wind Farm should be scrapped, citing concern from communities about the workers camp and the project. While calling for a duplication of Cogan Creek Power Station to support the Western Downs Digital Park, he said renewable projects should not "litter the landscape" and take "away our food security". He suggested a range of options should be on the table to manage the energy demands of hyper-scale data centres. "I think we've got the opportunity to get this right with baseload power, gas, coal, nuclear — if we're brave enough, and I think we should be brave enough — and put all the options on the table because this is the new frontier," Mr Littleproud said. "This is the next industrial revolution. We can't put our heads in the sand and go, 'This is all going to go away.' It's not." Two wind turbines projects on the Western Downs have been called-in by the state government to assess whether they go ahead or not. ( ABC News: Nathan Morris ) Queensland Treasurer and Energy Minister David Janetzki said the state government was committed to renewable energy projects, adding that Queensland had more large-scale wind and solar projects committed to than anywhere else in Australia. Mr Janetzki said the state's energy plan was "all about the getting the balance right" between coal, gas and private-sector-investment renewable projects, which included the Tarong West Wind Farm. "We've got applications processes and we've given the community a chance to have their say, and that's an important process," he said. "We're open for business and that means renewable in the private sector and that's an important thing to make clear. "That shows we have a balanced approach and that'll be our approach for any future data centre proposals.

events.title: Shein, Temu shoppers do not feel responsible for environmental concerns, study finds
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Ultra-fast fashion buyers feel a lack of personal responsibility despite environmental concerns A new study of ultra-fast fashion buyers found price was one of the biggest shopping motivators. ( AP: Richard Drew ) Shoppers of ultra-fast fashion companies, such as Shein and Temu, say despite being aware of environmental and ethical concerns, other factors such as price, convenience and not feeling personally responsible keep them coming back. A new study published in the Journal of Global Fashion Marketing this week found millennials, who frequently expressed concern about ethical and sustainability issues, often did not translate this concern into purchasing behaviour. The study surveyed 20 Australian millennials who shopped on ultra-fast fashion sites about what informed their purchasing behaviours. It found affordability, convenience, promotions, social media trends, novelty, variety and social validation were the biggest purchase drivers. For some, affordability meant they were likely to purchase styles they may not usually try and make riskier choices. You can get five things for the price of one at other places. I can redo my wardrobe every season without hurting my bank account. It's perfect when I need something quick and cheap for an event. The study also found the purchases were usually not spontaneous, with many shoppers saying they saved carts and waited for a sale before purchasing. When I see a 70 per cent off notification, it's almost impossible not to look. It feels like I'm losing money if I don't buy it. Sales get me every time. I've bought outfits I didn't even wear just because they were on sale. I add things to my cart and wait for payday or a discount notification. Study co-author Carol Tan, who is an associate professor at the School of Fashion and Textiles at RMIT University, said this behaviour was known as "strategic spontaneity". "You think it's impulsive, but it's actually planned," she said. "So what people do is they save the items, they have a wish list, and then they monitor their sales and wait for payday. "It could be sitting in their cart for a week or a month, and then a spur-of-the-moment decision is when they actually make the purchase and it happens in minutes." Contact Liana Walker at walker.liana@abc.net.au The fast and ultra-fast fashion gap While fast fashion has been around for some time, platforms such as Shein and Temu differ in their production and distribution methods. Traditional fast-fashion brands release a new collection every two to four weeks that can range from hundreds to thousands of styles and sell primarily through physical stores. Ultra-fast fashion stores produce 2,000 to 10,000 new styles daily and use digital-only, mobile app-dominant sales models. Dr Tan said the rise of ultra-fast fashion has pushed some fast-fashion brands to change their strategy. "They are trying to not compete with the Sheins of the world and they are trying to go a bit more upmarket. So they sell better-quality stuff and they have like $400 jackets," she said. Outside of the growing price gap between fast fashion and ultra-fashion fashion, Dr Tan said these sites often sold items you could not buy in brick-and-mortar stores. Despite participants expressing concerns about the environmental and ethical impacts of ultra-fast fashion brands, many still continued to purchase on Shein or Temu. According to the latest figures from the Australia Institute, on average Australians purchase 56 items of clothing a year. It also reports more than 200,000 tonnes of clothing end up in Australian landfills each year. The study found participants were more influenced by social and economic drivers than long-term ethical concerns. I know it's bad for the planet, but when I'm on a budget and need an outfit for Saturday, I just block that out. I try to buy sustainable brands, but they are so expensive. Shein is just there and it's easy. If the big brands are allowed to sell it, then it can't be all my fault for buying it. I feel bad sometimes, but one small top isn't going to destroy the ocean. The study also found buyers would draw on explanations such as reduced feelings of personal responsibility, affordability constraints, limited access to sustainable alternatives and the belief that the individual purchases had little impact. In some countries, different taxes have been introduced to deter buyers from ultra-fast fashion brands. France has banned advertising from ultra-fast fashion businesses and introduced a fee that will rise to €10 ($16) per item by 2030. New Zealand has a levy of NZ$2.21 ($1.80) per package.

events.title: Charity provides school lunches for kids as food insecurity rises
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts National school lunch program launched in Moe aims to tackle food insecurity Victoria and Brandon are big fans of the Spoonfull program. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) A new universal school meals program launched in Moe offers healthy lunches to primary school children. The program aims to tackle food insecurity as well as improving student wellbeing and learning outcomes. The charity Eat Up hopes to roll out the program across Australia to schools in need. It is lunchtime at Elizabeth Street Primary School at Moe in Victoria's east. On today's menu, a chicken pasta bake is the hot option, and tuna and salad rolls are on offer for others. The children queuing up are told that the more they can stack on their plates, the better. "I love the food, it's amazing," student Victoria says. "My favourite has been the lasagne and butter chicken, and I really like the wraps they make. "They give options to us that if we don't like a food, then we can just try it and I just love how they do that." A team of volunteers helps to prepare the students' lunches. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) The lunches are part of a program that aims to tackle child hunger and improve student wellbeing across the country. The charity Eat Up has launched its pilot program Spoonfull at the school, a universal meal program that provides every student at participating schools with a healthy lunch, every day. Ian Frost and Carol O'Reilly say they have seen a huge improvement since the program was introduced. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) The program was officially launched at Elizabeth Street Primary School in its purpose-built Hearts and Hands Learning Kitchen, after some strong lobbying by the school's wellbeing officer Carol O'Reilly. "I could see a need. I've been at this school for 17 years and I noticed running [the school's] breakfast club that kids are coming in without sandwiches," Ms O'Reilly said. "Now I know they're going out for recess with a full belly." She said learning outcomes and student welfare had improved greatly since the introduction of the program. "The kids are smiling. You can see them outside, they're playing and they're just dying to know what's for lunch." Students are offered a variety of healthy foods, including a hot lunch. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) School principal Ian Frost said the school lunch program had a positive impact on what students eat and had led to improved wellbeing and academic performance. Eat Up has been running for 15 years, delivering more than 6 million free on-demand school lunches to children experiencing food insecurity. Charity founder Lyndon Galea said the Spoonfull program built upon that business model to offer something more sustainable for schools to support students long-term. "This is different to our core model, [where] we have on-demand lunches, in terms of the cheese sandwiches, yoghurts and recess snacks," Mr Galea said. "We've learnt of certain schools where there's perhaps a higher number of kids arriving without food from home or where the socio-economic need bites even harder," he said. Lyndon Galea founded Eat Up 15 years ago. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) At Elizabeth Street Primary School, Spoonfull helped fund upgrades to the school kitchen to have commercial fridges and ovens, with hopes of also installing a dishwasher. Young people pushing back against artificial intelligence Rare century-old Mildura housing scheme directs lease revenue to local schools Loophole closed after rare private prosecution shuts Hepburn council Wilsons Prom's Sealers Cove track reopens after five years According to Australian Bureau of Statistics data from 2023, about 16 to 22 per cent of Australian children experience food insecurity. Single-parent households and low-income families were at the highest risk. As the cost of living continues to affect families, so too has the growth in food insecurity. "Families who are already in a difficult spot are needing help more often and then a lot of families who have historically been just above that level of need and needing support are accessing food support for the very first time," Mr Galea said. Through support from Spoonfull, the school was able to make key upgrades to its kitchen. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) Eat Up hopes to have enough support to roll out similar pilots in two additional schools. "I think it would be phenomenal for Australia and something our country can really take a big step forward [in]," Mr Galea said. Elizabeth Street Primary School student Victoria agreed and said she thought all schools could benefit from the program.
